strengths: Clear architectural design combining segment-level recurrence, layer-local memory tracks, bidirectional cross-attention (read and write), and an LRU-based update/rewrite mechanism.

Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple domains with distinct memory demands: synthetic memory diagnostics (T-Maze up to 1,000,000 steps), control/puzzles (POPGym), and visual manipulation tasks (MIKASA-Robo).

Consistently strong empirical performance against relevant sequence and offline baselines (DT, RATE, DMamba, BC-LSTM, Diffusion Policy), demonstrating remarkable extrapolation capabilities on long sequences.
Detailed ablation study exploring the effects of memory size, blending rate, initialization scale, positional relative bias, and the LRU policy.
weaknesses: Mismatch between title/framing and experimental methodology: The title highlights 'LONG-HORIZON RL', but the entire method is trained via supervised imitation learning / Behavior Cloning on offline expert demonstrations (Section 5.1 and Appendix A.6). No reinforcement learning update rule or RL training algorithm is used for ELMUR.

The theoretical contributions in Section 4 (Propositions 1 and 2) are quite elementary, consisting of standard geometric series decay and triangle inequality bounds for convex combinations, and are somewhat overstated as formal retention/stability analysis.
Inconsistency in POPGym reporting: Section 5 and Table 2 refer to 48 POPGym tasks, but Table 4 is captioned 'Across 21 partially observable tasks...' and lists only 21 tasks.

High hyperparameter sensitivity: Figure 6 shows that when memory capacity is constrained ($M < N$), performance drops significantly and becomes fragile to the blending factor $\lambda$ and initialization $\sigma$. Furthermore, Table 5 reveals that hyperparameters such as $\lambda$ vary drastically across tasks (from 0.05 to 0.90), suggesting careful manual tuning is required.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated architecture: Augmenting each transformer layer with a dedicated, persistent memory track via bidirectional cross-attention (mem2tok and tok2mem) and an LRU-managed update rule is a conceptually sound and practical approach to handling long-horizon POMDPs.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The paper evaluates across three diverse domains—synthetic stress tests (T-Maze), pixel-based robotic manipulation (MIKASA-Robo), and a broad suite of partially observable tasks (48 POPGym environments)—demonstrating consistent gains over baselines such as RATE, Decision Transformer, and BC-LSTM.

Remarkable sequence extrapolation: Achieving 100% success on T-Maze corridors up to one million steps when trained on context lengths of only L=10 with S=3 segments convincingly demonstrates the efficacy of the segment-level recurrence and bounded memory mechanism.

Detailed ablation studies: The ablations thoroughly examine the influence of memory capacity M, blending factor λ, initialization scale σ, relative biases, layer-local vs. shared memory, and MoE vs. standard FFN layers, giving clear insights into the stability and operational envelope of the model.
weaknesses: Positioning mismatch between title ('Long-Horizon RL') and methodology: While the paper frames the problem in POMDP terms and includes RL references, the core methodology and experimental setups are strictly offline supervised learning (behavior cloning on pre-collected expert trajectories). No actual reinforcement learning algorithm (policy gradient, Q-learning, or reward optimization) is proposed or directly coupled with ELMUR.

Trivial theoretical analysis: Propositions 1 and 2 (exponential forgetting rate and boundedness of memory embeddings) are elementary consequences of convex combinations and standard induction/triangle inequality. Presenting them as core theoretical contributions overstates their mathematical depth.

Brittleness under under-provisioned memory: The ablation results in Figure 6 show that when memory capacity is smaller than the required segments (M < N), performance is highly sensitive to the blending parameter λ, and intermediate blending (λ ≈ 0.4–0.6) causes significant performance degradation. This suggests that the convex blending mechanism may struggle with effective lossy compression when memory capacity is tight.

Lack of physical real-world robot experiments: While MIKASA-Robo provides visual manipulation tasks, the evaluation remains entirely in simulation. Given the motivation centered on real-world robotics in the introduction, validation on a real robotic platform or addressing real-world perceptual drift would substantially strengthen the work.

strengths: Well-motivated and clear architectural design combining layer-local memory, bidirectional cross-attention (mem2tok and tok2mem), and an LRU-based update/rewrite mechanism.

Extensive empirical evaluation across diverse domains: extreme-horizon synthetic tasks (T-Maze up to 10^6 steps), vision-based continuous robotic manipulation (MIKASA-Robo), and the standard POPGym benchmark (48 tasks).
Strong performance gains over standard sequence modeling and offline policy baselines (such as Decision Transformer, RATE, BC-LSTM, and Diffusion Policy), particularly in memory-demanding settings.

Thorough ablation study analyzing critical architectural choices, including memory size M versus required segments N, blending parameter lambda, layer-local vs. shared memory, and the impact of the LRU eviction policy.
weaknesses: Mismatch between the title/framing ('for Long-Horizon RL') and the actual methodology: the paper primarily trains models via supervised Imitation Learning (Behavior Cloning on expert demonstrations) rather than reinforcement learning algorithms (e.g., actor-critic or Q-learning).

The theoretical contributions in Section 4 (Propositions 1 and 2) are elementary algebraic unrollings of standard convex combinations and basic norm bounds via the triangle inequality; framing these as formal theoretical guarantees overstates their depth.

Memory is detached across segments during training (no BPTT across segment boundaries), but there is insufficient discussion of how this truncated gradient flow affects the ability of the write mechanism (tok2mem) to learn optimal long-horizon compression without long-term credit assignment signals.

Hyperparameters (such as memory size, LRU blending rate, and architecture depth) differ significantly across benchmarks (Table 5), suggesting that performance can be sensitive to task-specific manual tuning.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated architectural design: ELMUR integrates layer-local external memory with bidirectional cross-attention (mem2tok and tok2mem) and an LRU-based convex update mechanism, providing an effective and bounded solution for long-horizon context retention.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across diverse domains: The model is benchmarked on synthetic tasks (T-Maze up to 1,000,000 steps), control and puzzle benchmarks (all 48 tasks of POPGym), and vision-based robotic manipulation (32 tasks in MIKASA-Robo), consistently matching or outperforming strong baselines such as RATE, DT, and Diffusion Policy.

Insightful mechanistic analysis: The paper includes extensive probing, attention visualization, and PCA analysis (Appendix A.9–A.11) demonstrating that the network indeed writes relevant task cues into specific memory slots and maintains them across long horizons without drift.
Solid ablations: The ablation study clearly investigates the role of relative positional bias, LRU management, layer-local vs. shared memory, memory capacity M, and the blending factor lambda.
weaknesses: Misalignment between framing and learning paradigm: While the title and framing emphasize 'Long-Horizon RL Problems', the method is primarily evaluated as an offline sequence modeling / Behavior Cloning (imitation learning) architecture trained on expert demonstrations (with only D4RL trajectory conditioning explored in the appendix). Clarifying that this is an offline policy architecture would improve positioning.

Elementary theoretical analysis: Propositions 1 and 2 merely state basic algebraic properties of convex combinations / exponential moving averages and the triangle inequality. While helpful for intuition, they offer limited theoretical depth.

Zero success rates on complex sequential tasks: On several challenging compositional MIKASA-Robo environments (BunchOfColors, SeqOfColors, ChainOfColors), ELMUR as well as all baselines score 0.00, showing that compositional multi-phase reasoning remains an open challenge not resolved by this architecture.
Limited online interaction: The method is not evaluated in an active online RL setting where memory must adapt during exploratory data collection rather than static demonstration trajectories.

strengths: Clear motivation addressing a fundamental challenge: long-horizon credit assignment and context retention in partially observable decision-making tasks without incurring quadratic attention overhead.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning multiple benchmark suites with diverse characteristics: synthetic long-corridor T-Maze (extrapolating up to 10^6 steps), robotic manipulation with visual observations (MIKASA-Robo across 32 tasks), and the diverse POPGym suite (48 tasks), supplemented by D4RL and ViZDoom experiments.
Strong empirical gains over competitive baselines (e.g., RATE, Decision Transformer, DMamba, Diffusion Policy), notably achieving a 70% relative improvement in aggregate success rate on MIKASA-Robo.

Thorough ablation and interpretability studies, including post-hoc linear/non-linear probing of memory embeddings, PCA visualization of memory trajectories, slot variance tracking, and cross-attention map analysis demonstrating functional memory allocation.
weaknesses: The theoretical contributions in Section 4 are overstated. Proposition 1 simply unrolls a standard scalar exponential moving average (EMA) recurrence, and Proposition 2 is a direct application of the triangle inequality for convex combinations; while correct, these are elementary properties rather than deep theoretical insights.

Memory hyperparameters vary significantly across tasks without an automated selection principle. As shown in Table 7, memory size M ranges from 2 to 256 and blending parameter lambda ranges from 0.05 to 0.9 depending on the environment. Furthermore, ablation results (Figure 6) show high sensitivity when memory capacity is constrained (M < N).

In MIKASA-Robo (Table 8), 9 out of 32 environments yield 0.00 success rates across all evaluated methods (e.g., BunchOfColors, SeqOfColors, ChainOfColors suites). A clearer discussion or diagnosis of the failure mode on these complex sequential tasks would provide valuable context.

Architectural confounding: The model integrates several components simultaneously (segment recurrence, layer-local slots, bidirectional cross-attention, relative bias, LRU management, and DeepSeek-MoE FFNs). Although Table 3 ablates several of these, the inclusion of MoE layers in what is fundamentally a memory architecture study complicates the core narrative, especially given that MoE -> MLP ablation shows identical task performance.

strengths: Well-motivated and cleanly formulated architecture: Integrating layer-local external memory with bidirectional cross-attention (mem2tok and tok2mem) and an LRU convex-blending update rule is conceptually neat, scalable, and avoids the quadratic overhead of standard long-context transformers.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: Evaluated across a wide variety of benchmarks testing different aspects of memory (extreme extrapolation in T-Maze up to 10^6 steps, 48 diverse tasks in POPGym, 32 vision-based robotic manipulation tasks in MIKASA-Robo, 3D visual navigation in ViZDoom, and MDP sanity checks in D4RL).

Strong empirical results: ELMUR substantially outperforms prior methods on long-horizon partially observable tasks, e.g., improving aggregate success on MIKASA-Robo by ~70% over the previous best memory-augmented baseline (RATE) and achieving top results on POPGym.

Insightful analysis and interpretability: The paper includes rigorous theoretical bounds (half-life and memory boundedness) along with in-depth probing, PCA visualizations, and cross-attention map inspections that clearly show the model performs targeted, sparse writes and preserves key task variables over extended horizons.
weaknesses: Offline/Imitation learning focus despite the title: While the title and abstract emphasize 'Long-Horizon RL Problems', the actual experimental regime is strictly offline sequence modeling / imitation learning from expert demonstrations. Validating whether ELMUR can be trained end-to-end via online RL or off-policy actor-critic RL under partial observability remains open.

Hyperparameter sensitivity: As shown in the ablation study and Appendix Table 7, critical hyperparameters such as memory size $M$ and the LRU blend factor $\lambda$ (ranging widely from 0.05 to 0.9 across tasks) require careful configuration depending on the task's temporal structure and sequence segmentation.

Failure on complex multi-step memory tasks: On MIKASA-Robo tasks requiring chaining multiple memory items (such as BunchOfColors, SeqOfColors, ChainOfColors), ELMUR, like all other baselines, achieves 0% success, highlighting remaining limits in retaining and composing complex sequential memory items.
